Hospital slashed costs, then a patient froze to death on its roof

By A Reporter
September 1, 2026

The hospital had been cutting costs for three years when the night shift found the roof access door propped open with a fire extinguisher, a detail that would later appear in four separate investigations and a wrongful-death suit filed by the family in the spring.

Staffing records reviewed for this story show the overnight census had been reduced from eleven nurses to six across the same period, while the number of admitted patients held roughly steady. Administrators described the change as a realignment and said it followed industry benchmarks that they declined to name.

Three former employees, each of whom left the hospital in the year before the death and none of whom was authorised to speak publicly, described a building in which alarms were routinely silenced because so many of them were faulty that responding to each one had become impossible on a six-nurse floor.

The patient was admitted on a Tuesday with confusion and a low-grade fever. By the following morning the room was empty, the bed was made, and no one had logged a discharge. The body was found eleven hours later by a contractor replacing a condenser unit on the north side of the roof.

What the records show

In a statement, the hospital said it had since installed door alarms on all roof accesses and retrained staff on elopement protocol. It declined to say whether overnight staffing had been restored to its previous level, citing the pending litigation.
